The court in *Jones v. 1.  **Express Waiver:** This class involves deeds or agreements where the surface owner explicitly and unequivocally waives their right to surface support. This landmark decision established that a witness may be cross-examined with respect to any immoral, vicious, or criminal act of their life that may affect their character and show them to be unworthy of belief. The purpose of this rule is to prevent the trial from being sidetracked by mini-trials on collateral issues that are not directly relevant to the facts in dispute. *United States v. Read*, decided December 23, 1985, and amended February 10, 1986, involved Jane Read appealing a judgment of conviction for wire fraud and conspiracy to commit wire fraud, entered upon her Alford plea on October 1, 1985. Read contended that the trial court abused its discretion in denying her presentence motion to withdraw her Alford plea. She also challenged the denial of release on bail pending appeal. Read was indicted on June 15, 1983, on four counts of fraud by wire. The case was heard by Circuit Judges Tang and Farris, and District Judge Kelleher.

Warren James Sharp appealed on four grounds, including that the district court erred in accepting his guilty plea because he did not understand the charges, and that the district court breached the plea agreement by sentencing him to fifteen years instead of the ten years recommended by the government. Sharp also argued that the government breached the agreement by not informing the court that he was less culpable than other codefendants. The case primarily presented the issue of whether restitution could be ordered for losses suffered by all victims of a wire fraud scheme when a guilty plea was accepted for only one count of the scheme.
